stem: Why is Wounded Knee usually treated as the end of the Indian wars?

stimulus.source_note: Photograph of the burial of Lakota dead at Wounded Knee, South Dakota, winter of 1890-1891. Public domain (Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons). Image viewed before writing.
stimulus.text: The photograph shows men loading Lakota dead onto a wagon at Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota, in the winter of 1890-1891, while soldiers on horseback watch from the ridge behind them. The dead were Lakota men, women, and children killed on December 29, 1890, when the Seventh Cavalry opened fire during the disarmament of Big Foot's band.

options.text: It was the largest battle ever fought on the Plains
options.misconception: Background: Little Bighorn and other fights were larger battles; Wounded Knee was the killing of a disarmed band, not a large battle.

options.text: It forced Congress to repeal the Dawes Act at once
options.misconception: Background: the Dawes Act stayed in force until the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.

options.text: After it, no Native nation could field an independent armed force
It ended all Native religious life on the reservations
options.misconception: Background: the Ghost Dance faded, but Native religious life continued on the reservations.

rationales.A: Background: Little Bighorn and other fights were larger battles. Wounded Knee was the killing of a disarmed band, not a large battle.
rationales.B: Background: the Dawes Act stayed in force until the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.
rationales.C: Background: by 1890 every Plains nation had been confined to reservations and the buffalo were gone. Wounded Knee killed the last band still resisting in arms, so organized military resistance effectively ended there.
rationales.D: Background: the Ghost Dance faded, but Native religious life continued on the reservations.
rationales.general:
Picture the last band still outside army control, surrounded on a frozen creek.
1. Ask what was left to resist with. Background: The nations were on reservations, the herds were gone, the chiefs were dead or captured.
2. Ask what the soldiers did. Background: They disarmed Big Foot's band and then opened fire.
3. Name the ending. Background: After this killing, no Native nation could still fight as an independent force.
Remember: a war ends when one side can no longer field an army, not when the last shot is fired.
